One of Bendel’s strongest codes was its original flagship store on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. A beautiful, jewellike building with 276 panels of glass commissioned from René Lalique in 1912, it is now a tarnished testament to retail’s incredible power to seduce, entertain, and educate. In 1985, Bendel was acquired by The Limited (the owner of Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works). The company expanded with new store openings across the country, but the shops felt nothing like the original iconic flagship; they felt more like typical Limited stores. At the time of the acquisition, Limited chairman Leslie Wexner said, “There is a potential for Bendel’s in every major city in the world.” In keeping with the growth strategies for other Limited-owned stores, Bendel’s twenty-eight stores were mall-based and lacking in character and sold accessories that were not sufficiently unique in their designs to set them apart from other major retailers, such as Macy’s and Saks Fifth Avenue. In 2009, the store stopped selling apparel entirely, and in 2014 it started to sell only Bendel-brand accessories. The appeal of Bendel’s original concept was based not on ubiquity or consistency but on its power of individuality and curation. Before it changed strategy, store buyers would scour the globe, dig for new and exciting ideas and designs, and then introduce up-and-coming designers and ideas to customers. The store’s later private label line was developed without the uniqueness and creativity of global designers. The search for design talent around the world ceased. The merchandising function was essentially relegated to where items sat on the selling floor and how they were priced. The magic was gone. The singularity ceased to exist. A typical retail management approach to what was a most atypical store experience killed Bendel. Clearly, accessories were where the retailer made money. However, other categories (such as fashion and beauty) provided dimension and richness to the store experience—and ultimately the customers who would have helped keep the store alive. The codeless, lackluster Albertsons supermarkets diminish any hope of intimacy with shoppers thanks to harsh lighting, rows and rows of generic products, conventional elevator music, clunky shopping carts, and employees clad in matronly navy blue aprons. The navigational ease and curatorial feel of its smaller boxes helps Trader Joe’s aesthetics, too, something traditional large supermarkets have a hard time competing with. There is a way for retail to succeed. People will always feel the need to touch, feel, and smell, and retail offers a place to do that. In finding a way to make in-store shopping a social experience that also offers a sense of discovery and uniqueness, retail can win. For the moment, at least, we cannot touch anything we’re looking at in an online store. For those trying to uncover codes—whether your company is a hundred years old or five—the first step is to do what I call a “brand audit.” Dive into your archives. The deeper your heritage, the more you have to work with, of course. For established companies, looking back into archives, as fashion houses often do, can be an eye-opening experience. This is an immersion into not just how your products historically were made and marketed but why they were made and marketed that way, how their expressions were influenced by the times, and, above all, how they evolved through history. Who was the founder? How was he or she affected by the times? What other forces were in play? How did your brand evolve amid changing circumstances and influences? What were the defining moments of the brand? From this you’ll start to see patterns emerge. You’ll see which expressions of the brand continued to resonate and which ones didn’t and how the company leadership, culture, and marketplace responded to different cues along the way. The archive might include samples or images of product designs (preferably chronologically presented, so the auditor can see how designs have evolved). But it should also include other visible elements (e.g., logos, mottos, ads, store plans). One method is to show unaffiliated or unbiased people an advertisement or marketing campaign for your brand, concealing all references to your brand’s name, logo, or specific products. See if they can identify your company based on the displayed elements (e.g., color palettes, material choices, fonts, voice/tone/sound, and even location). That is the ultimate litmus test for a power brand built on clear, consistent, and ownable codes. Even if your company has strong, identifiable codes and a solid position in the market, remember that markets are dynamic and customers continually form new judgments. Loyalists can move away, and over time, new customers must be enticed in order for a business to sustain and grow —and remain relevant. The balancing act between keeping long-standing customers happy and attracting new ones who may have different expectations from existing patrons is an issue for all businesses. In the next chapter, we examine this and other common challenges and the aesthetic solutions for addressing them. Chapter 4 Designed to Last Aesthetic Strategies for Common Business Challenges Though no two companies face identical problems, inhibitors to growth and viability tend to come in recognizable patterns. And many of them are best tackled through what I call “aesthetic solutions.” Of the Fortune 500 1, companies in 1955, only sixty remained on the list in 2018. 2 Why do so few companies sustain their success? I would argue that, in short, the vast majority of companies play a game that they cannot win. Target cannot beat Walmart at Walmart’s game, just as Yahoo! could not beat Google at Google’s game. Yet, unlike Yahoo!, Target has remained relatively strong by playing its own game. In looking at classic business challenges, the solutions are generally not found in business school case studies or best-selling business books, which are typically oriented around highly structured frameworks, analytic tools, and dispassionate views about the marketplace; they are found in a profound and empathic understanding of your customers—not what they buy or where they shop but how they feel and what delights them—and a vision of how their pleasure can be enhanced not as shoppers but as humans. According to Clayton Christensen, a professor of business administration at Harvard Business School and one of the world’s top experts on innovation and growth, when we buy something, we are in effect “hiring” it to help us do a job (whether that’s finding something to make us look sexy for a date or putting something tasty and healthy into our kid’s lunch box). If the product does the job successfully, we will “hire” it again (in other words, buy it again). If it fails, we fire it. 3 We buy things because we want or need them to help us succeed in our endeavors no matter how mundane or grand. In other words, people, not machines, buy things. People are emotional and make decisions largely based upon how their purchases make them feel. The better they feel, the more engaged and loyal they are toward those products and brands. Christensen says companies miss this (and fail) because they make product and marketing decisions based on what he sees are false correlations between a buyer’s attributes (status, age, job, gender) and his or her buying decisions. Regardless of what business you’re in, I would advise you—as I do all businesspeople—to bring as much of yourself—your values, your personality, your style, and even your quirks—into the equation as possible. The Commoditization Trap If you think selling products, in general, is challenging, try selling commodity products. Your only advantage may be your relatively low prices, and that advantage inevitably dwindles over time. However, some companies have succeeded in turning this seemingly intractable challenge —that of selling basic, nondifferentiated, interchangeable goods—into a unique, differentiated, and sustainable value proposition by designing an entirely new and exciting human experience built around their commodities. I call this strategy for shifting the focus from a low-value product to high-value experience the “Starbucks Solution.” Such commodity businesses, whether they are selling coffee, soybeans, or cement, have an opportunity to transform their entire business proposition through aesthetic strategies that create unique and exciting experiences and weave rich stories around their goods to generate buzz, desirability, and loyalty. Starbucks distinguished itself from traditional coffee shops by designing its interiors for comfort, not efficiency, and elevating its servers to “baristas,” conjuring European know-how and artisanship. What’s important here is not whether Starbucks is differentiated and relevant today —I would argue that its stores have failed to evolve with the times—but what we can learn from its original breakthrough and long-standing success. In the 1990s and early 2000s, Starbucks was seen as truly differentiated and pioneering. (The same, by the way, was true for McDonald’s in the 1960s and ’70s.) During Starbucks’s first expansion outside Seattle, in 1987, 5 no coffee chains were doing what Starbucks had so far achieved—becoming the desired “third place”—the space that is neither work nor home but where eating, drinking (coffee), meeting, thinking, and socializing happen in a community setting. 6 After several years of Starbucks’s success, even McDonald’s got into the act, recognizing the financial potential of coffeehouse aesthetics as well as the diminished appeal and lack of differentiation of fast-food burger chains, and started converting many of its eateries into McCafe’s, complete with warm colors, wood details, free Wi- Fi, and more comfortable seating to accommodate longer consumer stays. Whether the tactic worked is debatable. After all, McDonald’s simply started to play Starbucks’s game. The question today for both these companies—and others grappling with the commodity trap—is what they can do to transform their commoditized products and fatigued in-store experiences into a new proposition that delights customers in unexpected ways. Such companies are in or entering businesses in which where there are established practices and traditions, ways of selling and marketing, and big-name recognition. The challenge is to incorporate aesthetic value into the business such that it enhances and differentiates the brand position from the industry leader and attracts an entirely new set of customers. For example, Southwest Airlines competes successfully against behemoths such as American Airlines and Delta 7 through its unique design theme (“Without a heart, it’s just a machine”), incorporation of friendly colors (canyon blue and sunflower yellow), and personal tone with former slogans such as “Just plain smart” and “Grab your bag, it’s on!” Of course, the classic example in retail is Target versus Walmart. Clinique, which emphasized its technical benefits, never used models in its ads; its products themselves were the stars. Whereas Lauder’s beauty advisers were expected to project grace and style, Clinique’s advisers wore white lab coats and took a curative approach to customer education. Clinique also built an abacus-like contraption for its counters with which customers could diagnose their skin type: oily, dry, sensitive, or combination. Last, whereas the Lauder brand was built on its strong fragrances, all of the Clinique products were marketed as allergy tested and fragrance-free. Companies fall into one of three categories: rule makers, rule takers, and rule breakers. The rule makers (e.g., Home Depot, General Motors, Lego) win through size, scale, market share, and resources. The rule takers (e.g., Lowe’s, Chrysler, Dillard’s, Fisher-Price) simply follow in the path of the rule makers; they adopt the same strategies and target the same customers, but they do so without the strength or market power to win. The rule takers are forever relegated to the runner-up position, if they survive. It’s not that they can’t make money, but they are never seen as innovators or as offering a special and distinct experience, and the performance gap between them and the rule makers tends to widen over time. Examples of rule takers include May Department Stores, which eventually lost out to Macy’s; Office Depot, which lost to Staples; and Circuit City, which lost to Best Buy. Rule breakers, while much smaller and younger than rule makers, gain traction and build momentum through differentiation, innovation, experimentation, and speed. In essence, rule breakers redefine their entire business, as did Dyson, which changed the rules around hair dryers and, before that, around vacuum cleaners. If they are successful, over time rule breakers tend to become rule makers. For example, in the 1990s, MAC Cosmetics was disruptive to then leaders Estée Lauder, Clinique, and Lancôme in its presentation, communications, and positioning. Today MAC has grown to become the largest prestige makeup brand in the United States, but it is being disrupted by newer, more compelling concepts such as Fenty Beauty by Rihanna (thanks to the celebrity power of Rihanna herself), Huda Beauty (thanks to its founder, Huda Kattan, a megainfluencer on social media), and Kat Von D (thanks to the highly original aesthetic and strong following of its inspiration behind the line, a famous tattoo artist). For all we know, a few years from now, the edgy streetwear brand Supreme may be a market leader in sportswear and will find itself fending off a new generation of rebellious players that are today just a faraway dream of some Parsons School of Design student or aspiring performer. The beer maker Stroh Brewery Company’s problems stemmed from bad management and a whirlwind of dubious acquisitions—and of course, inattention to the legacy that had made it relevant to beer drinkers. Founded in Detroit by a German immigrant, Bernhard Stroh, in 1850, by 1980, Stroh had become the third-largest brewery in the United States. 16 The founder’s great-grandson Peter Stroh became CEO that year and went on a shopping spree: he bought the F. & M. Schaefer Brewing Company and Joseph Schlitz Brewing Company. The company did not have the marketing or logistical firepower to manage so many disparate brands—brands that had nothing to do with its own culture and story. Other acquisitions followed, and they were also disasters. The company brought in an advertising expert, who promptly changed the company’s recognizable label, raised prices, and ended a long-standing “15 bottles for $12” deal. As a result, sales dropped 40 percent in one year. 17 After a while, the company didn’t even know if it could pay the interest on its bills. It had to start selling itself off in pieces. That downfall was not inevitable simply because it was a family-owned business operating at a time of corporate consolidation. Family-owned regional brewers including Yuengling and Schell’s Brewery were and are thriving. The owners of Stroh’s biggest competitor during the 1980s and 1990s, Coors Brewing Company, remain in the top hundred on the Forbes “America’s Richest Families” list. 18 In 1999, after 149 years in business, the Los Angeles–based Pabst Brewing Company ended up acquiring many of the company’s brands, including Colt 45 malt liquor, Lone Star, Schaefer, Schlitz, Schmidt’s, Old Milwaukee, Old Style, Stroh’s, and St. Ides. 19 The Miller Brewing Company bought the rest of the company’s brands. In 2016, the beer maker did a deep dive into its heritage, seeing that craft beer enthusiasts might also develop a taste for retro classics. Today SMEG is run by the third generation of Bertazzonis and maintains its heritage in many ways, starting with its Italian name SMEG, or Smalterie Metallurgiche Emiliane Guastalla—in English, the Guastalla Emilia Enamel Works. SMEG anticipated the desire for home comforts that increased affluence would bring in the 1950s and 1960s and as a result began specializing in home appliance manufacturing. When companies become trapped by their historic success, they lose touch with the aesthetic sensibilities, preferences, and demands of their current customers. In essence, they grow insular and fail to possess the level of aesthetic empathy needed to evolve. It is not enough to have a highly developed aesthetic sensibility. That is empathy: the ability to perceive, envision, and appreciate the emotional responses to and preferences of others for external stimuli. Without empathy you can’t effectively revisit, revise, and continually improve what you are doing—what the Japanese call kaizen. No Room to Roam What is the aesthetic process for building a new, captive, and loyal customer base, notwithstanding all the competitive pressures and “noise” in the marketplace? The challenge facing most upstarts, especially in the small consumer goods arena, is that they find themselves competing in ever more crowded, competitive, and mature sectors. Yet some new companies, including the eyeglasses maker Warby Parker and the clothing brand Everlane, have managed to break through the clutter. As of this writing, Warby Parker has an estimated worth of about $1 billion. 25 It’s big today, but it started out as an idea of four business school students who wondered why eyeglasses, little pieces of plastic, were so expensive. Answering that question led to an epiphany about how they could sell fashionable specs at a much lower price. It turned out that the same company, Luxottica, that owns the eyeglasses giant LensCrafters, also owns Pearle Vision, Ray-Ban, and Oakley, as well as the licenses for all Chanel and Prada prescription frames and sunglasses, and many other brand-name glasses. 26 Warby Parker’s founders felt that bypassing retailers and their middlemen could save consumers the 300 percent markup that occurs when eyeglasses are sold in a store. For people who like to buy designer eyewear brands such as Chanel, Luxottica pays the brand a licensing fee, adding even more of a premium onto the retail price tag. The popularity of brand-name eyeglasses gave the founders of Warby Parker a big hint in terms of succeeding in the eyeglasses business: they would have to pay attention to customers’ aspirations to create an elevated experience of buying glasses. “How do customers shop for glasses. First and foremost, they check do these look good on your face. So we’re a fashion brand first,” cofounder Neil Blumenthal told Forbes. 27 The eyeglasses are fashionable and fun, and the buying experience is great. You order five frames, which are delivered to you for free with return postage included. Then you can try them on, ask your friends how you look in them, pick one, and send them all back along with your prescription. Days later your new glasses arrive—at a fraction of the price of retail. And although price certainly addresses a nagging question everyone who wears glasses has asked at one time or another (why does this lump of plastic cost so much?), it’s the experience and the hip look of the glasses and the way customers can experience them that have catapulted Warby Parker into a segment of its own. The direct-to-consumer fashion house Everlane wrapped up 2016 with $100 million in revenue, not bad for a start-up that sells basics such as T- shirts, shift dresses, pullover sweaters, and blue jeans. 28 Its aesthetic magic is found not in its timeless silhouettes but in the way the company addresses the desires of its target market, millennials. The idea is that this demographic wants to know where its clothing comes from and how it’s made. As a result, Everlane provides shoppers a breakdown of what items are made of, where they are made, and how much it costs to produce them. You can follow a link to the factory where clothes are made to inspect the working conditions. 29 Everlane also uses social media platforms where millennials are prone to be found, such as Snapchat and Instagram, to talk about its manufacturing processes, answer questions, and show off “street fashion,” real customers wearing Everlane clothing in various cities and towns. As a result, the company is a master of engagement and transparency (or the illusion of it), which resonates with customers in ways that take them beyond a simple black T. These brands masterfully create moments for customers—experiences that differentiate their value propositions from that of more conventional players in highly competitive sectors. Their engagement goes well beyond the design of sellable products, their features and functionality; it is built on experiences that foster a sense of community and feed curiosity and connection among buyers. An Industrial Dilemma This set of challenges pertains to companies in industrial goods, which are made and marketed on the basis of their utility. People who buy such goods primarily want them to be effective and to last because replacement of such products comes at a high price. Most of us don’t want to have to replace our SUV each year, nor do we want to install an oven every six months or paint our living rooms on a sixty-day schedule. Some companies, including Dyson (vacuum cleaners), Viking (stoves), Yeti (coolers), Harry’s (razors), Benjamin Moore (paint), and Porcelanosa (floor tile), have used aesthetic models to create brands that are sought and valued for far more than their products’ features and functionality. The aesthetics of utility is so paramount to Dyson that it recently announced it would no longer develop plug-in vacuum cleaners but would focus its innovation efforts on cordless and robotic varieties and features. 30 Most of us know what it’s like to tangle a vacuum cleaner cord around a table leg, suck it into the mouth of the cleaner, or trip over it. It’s annoying. It prevents many people I know from even bothering to drag a vacuum cleaner out of the closet unless it is absolutely necessary for their well- being. Cordless and robotic vacuum cleaners have been a boon to cleaning people and homeowners everywhere—combined with Dyson’s strong sucking technology (a feature it first marketed, a vacuum cleaner that would not lose suction), the company really came to the rescue for those of us who want cleaning and maintenance to be simple and quick. This is the epitome of empathy—creating a product not because it’s easy for Dyson but because it makes cleaning easy and even enjoyable for its customers. The brilliance of Yeti is its ability to turn a banal camping and hunting and fishing accessory—a cooler—into a true object of desire. The product is so effective (even a starving grizzly bear can’t break into the cooler when locked) that customers brag about it for the company. They do the marketing for us. Yeti is really not about coolers, however. It’s about the great outdoors and preserving the natural world. It’s about sportsmanship and the wilderness.

We want to please you on as many levels as we can.” The Ethics of Aesthetics As a parent of two teenagers, I’m concerned about the temptations that bombard them every day. The couple also spent $35 million to sponsor research so they could make claims about POM’s health benefits. 42 In 2010, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a complaint against the Resnicks along with some of their business partners and two of their companies for deceptive trade practices, including misleading claims that the juice would prevent heart attacks, prostate cancer, and erectile dysfunction. In 2012, the FTC issued a cease-and-desist order, ruling that POM lacked credible scientific evidence that the juice and the dietary supplements could prevent any of the diseases they claimed to. 43 It turned out that POM Wonderful wasn’t so wonderful after all. In 2013, the Kellogg Company agreed to pay $4 million to settle a class action lawsuit over marketing claims it had made in 2009 for its Frosted Mini-Wheats, which were that consumption of the cereal increased children’s attention spans by almost 20 percent. 44 The FTC said the studies cited in the advertisement actually showed that the children who ate the cereal for breakfast averaged just under 11 percent greater attentiveness than children who ate no breakfast at all. Moreover, relatively few of the study’s participants reached anywhere near the 20 percent more attentive mark. Michael Moss wrote in his book Salt Sugar Fat: How the Food Giants Hooked Us that the clinical study Kellogg talked about in its ads (a study paid for by Kellogg) didn’t support even the most minimal claims. “The truly remarkable aspect of the campaign is that the company study, even if taken at face value, did not come close to supporting the claim in its advertising. Half of the children who ate bowls of Frosted Minis showed no improvement at all on the tests they were given to measure their ability to remember, think, and reason, as compared with their ability before eating the cereal.” 45 Kellogg wanted to create an “aesthetic of health” around what is basically a sugary and carb-heavy cereal—and surprisingly, like the Resnicks in their claims about POM Wonderful, failed to appreciate that most false claims are eventually exposed and undermine the brand’s integrity. In the long run, true aesthetic value can only be built on pure intentions and defensible actions.
